VII.1.title: A transmitter, not a maker
VII.1.reflection: Confucius describes himself as one who passes on rather than creates, trusting and loving the ancient ways, and compares himself to Old Peng, a figure from the distant past. It is a modest claim. The later tradition made him the founder of a school, which this chapter says he did not set out to be.
VII.1.question: What do you pass on that you did not make?

VII.2.title: Which of these is mine?
VII.2.reflection: To remember silently, to learn without tiring, to teach without wearying: which of these, Confucius asks, do I have? The question can be read as modesty or as a quiet claim to all three. VII.33 returns to the same two habits.
VII.2.question: Which of the three comes most easily to you?

VII.3.title: What worries me
VII.3.reflection: Virtue not cultivated, learning not discussed, hearing what is right and not moving toward it, not changing what is not good: these are the Master's worries. They are all failures of follow-through.
VII.3.question: Which of the four is your own worry?

VII.4.title: At leisure
VII.4.reflection: At home and at ease, the Master was relaxed and cheerful. The disciples recorded not only what he taught but how he looked when he was not teaching.
VII.4.question: How do you look when no one needs anything from you?

VII.5.title: No longer dreaming of the Duke
VII.5.reflection: How I have declined, Confucius says; for a long time I have not dreamed of the Duke of Zhou, the founder of the institutions he loved. Old age is felt as the loss of a dream.
VII.5.question: Whom or what did you once dream of that you no longer do?

VII.6.title: Four directions
VII.6.reflection: Set your will on the Way, base yourself on virtue, rely on ren, and take your ease in the arts. The four lines move from aim to footing to support to recreation. The arts here are ritual, music, archery, driving, writing and counting.
VII.6.question: Where do you take your ease?

VII.7.title: A bundle of dried meat
VII.7.reflection: From anyone who brought even a small bundle of dried meat as a gift, the customary token for a teacher, Confucius never refused instruction. The door was open to any who came with the smallest sign of wanting to learn.
VII.7.question: What small sign shows that you are ready to be taught?

VII.8.title: The other three corners
VII.8.reflection: Confucius does not open the way for someone who is not eager, nor prompt one who is not struggling to put it into words. If he shows one corner and the student cannot return with the other three, he does not repeat himself. Teaching requires effort from both sides.
VII.8.question: When were you last shown one corner and found the other three yourself?

VII.9.title: Beside a mourner
VII.9.reflection: Eating beside someone in mourning, he never ate his fill; on a day he had wept, he did not sing. Two small observances of fellow feeling. Grief, even someone else's, changes what one does.
VII.9.question: How do you change your conduct around someone who is grieving?

VII.10.title: No tiger without a weapon
VII.10.reflection: Confucius tells Yan Hui that only they two can take office when employed and withdraw when not. Zilu, wanting a share, asks whom the Master would take to lead an army. Not one who fights a tiger bare-handed or crosses a river without a boat and dies without regret, but one who goes into action with caution and a plan. Courage without care is not what he wants.
VII.10.question: Where are you brave in a way that is only careless?

VII.11.title: If wealth could be sought
VII.11.reflection: If wealth could be properly sought, Confucius says, he would do even the lowly job of holding a whip; if not, he follows what he loves. He is not against wealth, he is against pursuing it at any price.
VII.11.question: What would you do for money, and what would you not?

VII.12.title: Fasting, war, sickness
VII.12.reflection: The things he treated with the greatest care: fasting before sacrifice, war and illness. Each involves life and death, or the spirits, and none can be taken lightly.
VII.12.question: What in your life deserves more care than you give it?

VII.13.title: Three months without taste
VII.13.reflection: In Qi, Confucius heard the Shao music and for three months did not notice the taste of meat. He had not imagined music could reach such a height. The book records one experience of art so strong it displaced appetite.
VII.13.question: What work of art has affected you so strongly that it changed your ordinary days?

VII.14.title: The two brothers
VII.14.reflection: The disciples wonder whether Confucius supports the ruler of Wei, who was fighting his own father for the throne. Zigong asks instead about Bo Yi and Shu Qi, two brothers who each gave up a throne to the other. They sought ren and got it; why would they complain? Zigong comes out and says the Master is not for the ruler.
VII.14.question: When have you understood someone's answer to a question you did not ask directly?

VII.15.title: A bent arm for a pillow
VII.15.reflection: Coarse rice to eat, water to drink, a bent arm for a pillow: there is joy in these too. Wealth and honour gained wrongly are to him like floating clouds. It is one of the book's best-known pictures of contentment.
VII.15.question: What simple thing gives you joy?
VII.15.exercise: Find one ordinary pleasure today, a drink of water or a quiet minute, and notice it fully.

VII.16.title: Fifty years for the Changes
VII.16.reflection: Given more years, Confucius says, he would study the Yi, the Book of Changes, and might then be without great faults. The chapter is the main textual link between Confucius and the Changes. Some editions read a different character for Yi, and the line becomes "even so", without the book at all.
VII.16.question: What would you study if you were given more years?

VII.17.title: In the standard speech
VII.17.reflection: When he spoke of the Odes, the Documents and the observance of ritual, the Master used the standard pronunciation, the elegant speech of the court rather than his local dialect. Legge reads it as "his frequent themes". Either way, these were what he spoke of with care.
VII.17.question: What subjects do you speak of with special care?

VII.18.title: Forgetting old age
VII.18.reflection: The Duke of She asks Zilu about Confucius, and Zilu does not answer. Why not tell him, says the Master, that I am someone who forgets to eat in my eagerness, forgets my worries in my joy, and does not notice old age coming? It is the most cheerful self-portrait in the book.
VII.18.question: How would you want someone to describe you, if they had one sentence?

VII.19.title: Not born knowing
VII.19.reflection: I was not born knowing, Confucius says; I love the ancients and seek it diligently. He claims effort, not a gift.
VII.19.question: What do you know only because you worked to learn it?

VII.20.title: What he did not speak of
VII.20.reflection: The Master did not talk about prodigies, feats of strength, disorder or spirits. The list tells as much about him as any saying: his attention was on ordinary human conduct.
VII.20.question: What subjects do you choose not to talk about?

VII.21.title: Three walking together
VII.21.reflection: Walking with two others, I am sure to find my teacher among them: I follow their good points and correct in myself their bad ones. Every companion is a lesson, either way.
VII.21.question: What did the last two people you spent time with teach you?
VII.21.exercise: With the next two people you meet today, find one quality to follow and one to avoid.

VII.22.title: What can Huan Tui do to me?
VII.22.reflection: Huan Tui, a military officer of Song, tried to kill Confucius. Heaven gave me my virtue, the Master says; what can Huan Tui do to me? It is a moment of calm in danger, grounded in a sense of mission.
VII.22.question: What gives you steadiness when you are threatened?

VII.23.title: Nothing hidden
VII.23.reflection: Do you think I hide anything from you? I hide nothing; there is nothing I do that I do not share with you. The teacher answers a suspicion that he holds back secret teachings. His whole life is the lesson.
VII.23.question: Do the people close to you know how you actually live?

VII.24.title: Four things he taught
VII.24.reflection: He taught four things: culture, conduct, loyalty and good faith. Legge renders them as letters, ethics, devotion of soul and truthfulness. Two are learned in books and two only in life.
VII.24.question: Which of the four did your own education leave out?

VII.25.title: A man of constancy
VII.25.reflection: A sage I shall not see; a junzi would be enough. A good person I shall not see; someone constant would be enough. But pretending to have when one has not, to be full when empty, at ease when pressed: it is hard for such people to be constant. Pretence is the enemy of steadiness.
VII.25.question: Where are you pretending to more than you have?

VII.26.title: Not with a net
VII.26.reflection: The Master fished with a line but not with a net, and shot with an arrow but not at roosting birds. He took what he needed and left the rest a fair chance. Restraint applied even to sport.
VII.26.question: Where could you take less than you are able to?

VII.27.title: The second kind of knowing
VII.27.reflection: Some act without knowing; Confucius does not. He hears much, chooses the good and follows it, sees much and remembers it: this is the second kind of knowledge, below the knowledge one is born with. He places himself firmly in the second rank.
VII.27.question: How much of what you know did you choose deliberately, from many sources?

VII.28.title: The boy from Huxiang
VII.28.reflection: The people of Huxiang were hard to talk to, and the disciples are surprised that Confucius receives a boy from there. He approves of his coming forward, not of what he may do after; why be so severe? If someone purifies himself to come, accept the purity without vouching for his past.
VII.28.question: Whom do you refuse a fresh start because of where they come from?

VII.29.title: Is ren far away?
VII.29.reflection: Is ren far away? I wish for it, and here it is. After so many chapters where the Master refuses to call anyone ren, this one says it is as close as the wish. Both are true in the book: it is rare in a whole life and near in any moment.
VII.29.question: What good act is within reach of you right now?

VII.30.title: Fortunate to be corrected
VII.30.reflection: A minister of Chen asks whether Duke Zhao of Lu knew ritual, and Confucius says he did. Afterwards the minister points out that the duke married a woman of his own clan, against ritual, and disguised her name. Told of this, Confucius says: I am fortunate; if I make a mistake, people are sure to notice. He had defended his own ruler, and he accepts the correction gracefully.
VII.30.question: How do you respond when someone points out your mistake?

VII.31.title: Sing it again
VII.31.reflection: When someone sang well in his company, the Master would ask them to sing again and then join in. A small detail of pleasure in another's gift, and of joining rather than judging.
VII.31.question: Whose talent could you join in with, rather than only admire?

VII.32.title: Not yet a junzi in practice
VII.32.reflection: In learning I may be as good as others, Confucius says, but in practising what the junzi practises, I have not yet succeeded. He separates scholarship from conduct and grades himself low on the second.
VII.32.question: Which do you rate yourself higher in, knowing or doing?

VII.33.title: How could I dare?
VII.33.reflection: How could I dare call myself a sage or ren? It may be said only that I strive without tiring and teach without weariness. Gongxi Chi answers that this is exactly what the disciples cannot learn from him. The modest claim turns out to be the hardest.
VII.33.question: What do you do without tiring that others find hard?

VII.34.title: I have been praying a long time
VII.34.reflection: When the Master is gravely ill, Zilu asks to pray for him, citing a text of prayers to the spirits above and below. Is there such a thing? Confucius asks, and then says: my praying has been going on a long time. It may mean his whole life has been a prayer, or that he does not need Zilu's. The chapter keeps the ambiguity.
VII.34.question: What in your daily life could be called a kind of prayer?

VII.35.title: Extravagance and meanness
VII.35.reflection: Extravagance leads to arrogance, frugality to shabbiness; better shabby than arrogant. Of two faults, he prefers the one that harms others less.
VII.35.question: If you must err, which way do you err?

VII.36.title: Calm and anxious
VII.36.reflection: The junzi is calm and at ease; the small man is always anxious. The contrast is about inner weather, not outward fortune.
VII.36.question: What made you anxious today, and was it within your control?

VII.37.title: Gentle and firm
VII.37.reflection: The Master was gentle yet stern, commanding yet not harsh, respectful yet at ease. Each quality is held with its opposite. Book VII ends with a portrait, not a saying.
VII.37.question: Which pair of qualities would you most like to hold together?
